claims.text: The target material is a crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticle containing five or more metals.
Adding a minor element such as Cr can improve nanoparticle stability during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
Adding a minor element such as Cr can enhance catalytic performance.
The added minor element forms a stable solid solution with the nanoparticle alloy.
Cr addition can produce solid-solution hardening in a multielement alloy.
Cr addition can promote Laves-phase formation or precipitation in a multielement alloy.
Laves-phase precipitation can reduce atomic-radius misfit in a solid solution.
Laves-phase precipitation can lower the elastic energy of a solid solution.
Solid-solution hardening and Laves-phase precipitation will improve operational stability relative to nanoparticles without the minor-element addition.
The modified nanoparticles may retain enhanced catalytic performance at low noble-metal content.
The proposed scope is limited to near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
The proposed operating-temperature boundary is 773–1173 K.
The exact stabilization mechanism is uncertain.
The optimal minor-element composition is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The mediator proposes formation of a stable solid solution containing the added element, whereas the proposed Laves-phase mechanism entails partitioning and phase precipitation. These can coexist only if a stable solid-solution matrix plus a controlled secondary phase is intended, which is not stated.
